By Wednesday morning, 33 ballot measures restricting data center development had passed or were leading, according to the tracker Data Centers on the Ballot. Only one measure, in Harwood, North Dakota, went in favor of construction, and several races were still being counted. The local results came alongside wins for Democratic candidates who promised tighter rules on data centers. article_info.title: Voters back dozens of data center bans in midterms
article_info.summary: At least 33 local measures restricting data centers passed or led Wednesday, as Ohio drove the wave; just one backed construction.
article_info.bullet_summary:
- In the Nov. 3 midterms, voters approved bans, moratoriums and limits on data centers in at least 33 communities, according to Capacity[4].
- In **Ohio**, at least 14 municipalities passed bans or restrictions, including a Trenton measure blocking a proposed Amazon [Amazon.com, Inc.](pplx://entity_chip/2a215cce) campus, Fortune reported[5].
- Goldman Sachs [The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.](pplx://entity_chip/9b78accf) economists warned moratoriums could affect about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion, per Business Standard[9].

Voters in 18 Ohio municipalities decided 21 measures, and at least 14 municipalities passed bans or other restrictions. In Trenton, a ban on data centers larger than 25 megawatts passed with about 80% of the vote. The ban blocks the city's plan to annex land for a proposed 1,000-megawatt Amazon campus. In Ashville, about 82% of voters rejected a deal with developer EdgeConneX.[1][2][3]

The results reached well beyond Ohio. About 77% of voters in Edgewater, Florida, approved a ban, and 82% in Alhambra, California, supported one. Bloomington, Illinois, and the Maine towns of Peru and Wiscasset approved moratoriums. A pause in Emporia, Kansas, was leading with 60% in early returns.
